torso.title: Inside the Torso
torso.note: Illustrative layout of a typical humanoid torso, sized to fit this robot's shell. It is not an exact Unitree G1 teardown: the simulation model only includes the outer shell.

shell_front.title: Front Cover
shell_front.summary: The chest cover protects the electronics and gives the robot its look.
shell_front.role: Keeps out dust, fingers and debris, spreads the force of light impacts, and acts as a mounting surface for the chest panel.
parts: Injection-molded engineering plastic (PC/ABS or nylon) or thin aluminum
Vents where the cooling air enters
shell_front.connects: Screws onto the internal chassis. It doesn't carry the robot's weight; the frame does.
shell_front.sim: In the model this is a visual mesh plus a collision mesh. Its mass is folded into the torso link's total mass.

shell_back.title: Back Cover
shell_back.summary: The rear cover. It usually opens for battery swaps and service access.
shell_back.role: Gives access to the battery, connectors and the emergency-stop circuit without taking the robot apart.
shell_back.connects: Mounts to the back of the chassis rails.
shell_back.sim: Like the front cover: visual and collision geometry only, no separate physics body.

chassis.title: Internal Chassis (Spine)
chassis.summary: The metal skeleton inside the torso. It carries every load between the waist, shoulders and head.
chassis.role: Holds the arm motors at the shoulders and bolts to the waist actuator below. Everything else in the torso mounts to it.
chassis.connects: Waist joint below, both shoulder-pitch motors on the sides, head mount on top.
chassis.sim: The frame is why the torso is modeled as one rigid body: nothing inside it flexes enough to matter for control.

battery.title: Battery Pack
battery.summary: The robot's energy source and usually its heaviest internal part. Placing it low helps balance.
battery.role: Stores energy for every motor and computer. Its capacity sets how long the robot can run between charges.
parts: Cylindrical lithium-ion cells (e.g. 21700 format) wired in series-parallel
Nickel bus strips spot-welded between cells
battery.connects: Feeds the power distribution board through the BMS. Often hot-swappable through the back cover.
battery.sim: Its mass sits low in the torso, which lowers the robot's center of mass. Change the battery's mass in the model and you change how the robot balances.

bms.title: Battery Management System (BMS)
bms.summary: The battery's guardian: a circuit board that watches every cell.
bms.role: Measures each cell's voltage and temperature, balances the cells, estimates remaining charge, and disconnects the pack on over-current, over-heating or deep discharge.
parts: Microcontroller that reports state of charge
bms.connects: Sits on the pack. It reports to the main control computer over CAN or UART.
bms.sim: Not physically simulated, but battery level can be fed to a high-level planner, for example 'return to charger when below 20%'.

pdb.title: Power Distribution Board
pdb.summary: Splits battery power into the separate voltage rails the robot needs.
pdb.role: Sends high-voltage power to the joint motors and steps it down to lower voltages for the computers, sensors and fans.
parts: Thick copper bus bars and traces
Bulk capacitors that absorb current spikes when motors brake
pdb.connects: Battery in. Out: motor power trunks to each limb, low-voltage rails to the compute boards.
pdb.sim: Simulation assumes perfect power. On hardware, voltage sag during hard moves can reset a computer: a classic sim-to-real surprise.

estop.title: Safety Circuit (E-Stop)
estop.summary: A hardware kill switch that cuts motor power instantly, no matter what the software is doing.
estop.role: When the emergency stop is pressed (on the robot or a wireless remote), a relay physically cuts power to the motors.
parts: Watchdog circuit that trips if the controller stops responding
estop.connects: Sits between the power distribution board and the motor power trunks.
estop.sim: Simulation has no e-stop, which is exactly why every real robot test needs one. A policy that works in simulation can still behave unexpectedly on hardware.

control_computer.title: Real-Time Control Computer
control_computer.summary: Runs the fast, time-critical loops that keep the robot upright.
control_computer.role: Reads every joint encoder and IMU, estimates the robot's state, and sends motor commands hundreds of times per second, with strict timing.
parts: Embedded CPU (ARM or x86) running a real-time OS or kernel
Field-bus controller (EtherCAT or CAN) for talking to the motors
control_computer.connects: Talks to all 29 joint motors over the field bus. Receives joint targets from the AI computer.
control_computer.sim: In simulation the physics engine plays the role of the motors and sensors, and the same control code can run against it.

ai_compute.title: AI Compute Module
ai_compute.summary: The robot's AI brain. A Jetson-class module on a carrier board runs the neural networks.
ai_compute.role: Runs perception (detection, segmentation, depth processing), learned control policies and planning, using a GPU built for low-power inference.
parts: System-on-module: CPU + GPU + deep-learning accelerators + shared memory
Carrier board with camera inputs (MIPI CSI), PCIe, USB and Ethernet
Heatsink with fins, often with a heat pipe
ai_compute.connects: Cameras and LiDAR in. Joint targets out to the real-time control computer, about 50 times a second.
ai_compute.sim: Policies are trained on desktop GPUs in simulation, exported (for example to ONNX), then optimized (for example with TensorRT) to run on this module.

accelerator.title: AI Accelerator (NPU / TPU)
accelerator.summary: An optional add-on chip for running neural networks very efficiently.
accelerator.role: Takes over specific models, such as an always-on detector, so the main GPU stays free for other work. Uses less power per inference.
parts: M.2 card with a neural processing chip
accelerator.connects: Plugs into the carrier board's M.2 / PCIe slot.
accelerator.sim: To run on it, models are usually quantized (from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers). Check that accuracy holds after quantizing.

cooling.title: Cooling Fan
cooling.summary: Moves air through the torso so the computers and power electronics don't overheat.
cooling.role: Pulls air in through the front vents, past the heatsinks, and out the back.
cooling.connects: Powered from a low-voltage rail. Its speed is set from temperature sensors on the compute boards.
cooling.sim: Heat isn't simulated, but on hardware, thermal throttling slows down the AI computer and can delay control policies.

imu.title: Torso IMU Board
imu.summary: A small board with a gyroscope and accelerometer. It's the robot's sense of balance.
imu.role: Measures how the torso is rotating and accelerating, hundreds of times per second.
imu.connects: Bolted firmly to the chassis. Streams data to the real-time control computer.
imu.sim: This matches the real 'imu_in_torso' sensor site in the model. Its simulated readings include noise, just like real hardware.

comms.title: Communications Hub
comms.summary: The robot's internal network and its link to the outside world.
comms.role: Connects the computers to each other, and the robot to Wi-Fi or a tether for monitoring, teleoperation and cloud AI calls.
parts: Field-bus hub ports for the limbs
comms.connects: Links the AI computer, the real-time computer, the head sensors and the wireless link.
comms.sim: VELA's agent orchestrator would talk to the robot through a link like this. Network latency is why the LLM agents send high-level skill commands, never motor torques.

harness.title: Wiring Harness
harness.summary: The robot's nervous system and blood vessels: power and data cables running to every limb.
harness.role: Carries motor power (orange) and data (blue) from the torso to the shoulders, down through the waist, and up to the head.
parts: Cable routing through hollow joint shafts
harness.connects: From the power board and communications hub out to every limb.
harness.sim: Cables are left out of the simulation. On the real robot, cable stiffness and wear in joints that move a lot are a common reliability issue.
